output.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
output.body:
Scope creep is usually not a software problem. It is a decision problem.

If you are a small business owner trying to automate one workflow, the safest boundary is simple: one repeatable workflow, one measurable outcome, one fixed price for the pilot. Anything beyond that belongs in a later conversation, not in the middle of the build. That is not being difficult. It is how you keep the work inspectable.

The practical diagnostic question is: what is the one recurring workflow that costs time or creates risk, and how will you measure success in it? If you cannot answer that in plain English, the scope is still too loose. A good answer sounds specific: customer questions answered within a set time, invoices logged within a set time, leads recorded without manual cleanup. Those are examples, not promises.

Bareni’s normal sequence is a free 30-minute diagnostic, then a one-page pilot proposal with scope, price, and measures, then a working MVP within the intended scope. The timings are scopes, not guarantees. That structure makes creep visible early: if a new request appears, the right move is to say, “That is a separate workflow,” and decide whether it belongs in the next pilot.

The next step is boring in the useful way: pick one weekly workflow and write down its success measure before you talk about automation. Scope written late has a funny habit of becoming everyone’s problem.
